name: Kelly green
lede: Kelly green is the bright spring-grass green worn on St. Patrick's Day, a color named for an Irish surname and, by one account, only a century old.

sections.title: A recent name
sections.body:
St Clair writes that Kelly green emerged only at the beginning of the twentieth century [1]. Kelly is a common Irish surname whose origin is much disputed, with some scholars reading it as a warrior and others as a religious person [1]. Paterson gives the color a one-line entry, a strong mint green, and keeps it apart from the old English *Kendal green* [2]. Who first used the name is undocumented in our sources.

The early-twentieth-century date rests on St Clair alone [1].

sections.title: How Ireland turned green
sections.body:
The color's cultural weight is older than the name. Until the middle of the eighteenth century St Patrick was associated mainly with a shade of blue [1]. Irish Catholics then wanted a color of their own against the orange of William of Orange's Protestants, and the saint's shamrock, a trinity lesson, became central to Irish Catholic identity [1].

Green also had a French Revolution echo [1]. On 12 July 1789 Camille Desmoulins stuck a linden leaf in his hat, and the green cockade followed, until it was remembered that green was the livery of the Count of Artois, and the tricolor replaced it [1]. A green flag, sometimes with a golden harp, became the symbol of Irish Home Rule, and one flew beside the Union Jack at the Prince of Wales's visit in spring 1885 [1]. The Irish flag's green stands for Catholic nationalists, orange for Protestants, and white for hoped-for peace [1].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: Our swatch comes from web color lists and the ColorHub curriculum, not from a historical chart, so it fixes no 1900 color [3]. It is a vivid yellowish green, 5.5 CIEDE2000 units from the ISCC-NBS region of that name [3]. Paterson's mint is paler and cooler [2][3]. Neighbors are [[grass-green]], [[lime-green]] and [[shamrock-green]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The color is almost absent from museum paint. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in only one work, Gauguin's *Mother and Child under a Tree at Pont-Aven* of 1886, at 5.2 per cent [4]. It is rarer than 86 per cent of our named colors [4]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so read them as screen colors [4].
